title: A Rectangle the World Can Share
bigQuestion: How did a written kicking game become a rectangle two towns can share?

story.title: One Pitch, Two Languages
story.kicker: Two towns that do not share a language still share a rectangle.
paragraphs: A soccer pitch is a long rectangle with a goal at each end. Paint makes the room. The ball stays a ball. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
People kicked balls in streets and fields long before 1863. The Football Association meeting in London that year wrote one kicking code. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.

FIFA was founded in Paris in 1904. The first World Cup was played in Uruguay in 1930. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together. The names, the place, and the year stay on the page.
Illinois schools later joined IHSA soccer series. Boys crowned a first champion in 1972. Girls crowned a first champion in 1988. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
story.think: What has to travel with the ball so two towns can play?

lessons.title: Folk Football
lessons.mainIdea: People in many countries played kicking and carrying games before anyone wrote the 1863 laws.
reading: Village games in Britain used a ball and a crowd. Some games allowed carrying. Some banned it. Shrove Tuesday football is one famous seasonal match.
Those games had local customs, not one world book. A visitor from the next county might not know the local line.
The 1863 meeting did not invent kicking. It tried to write one set of words for clubs that wanted the same kicking game.

words.d: older local kicking or carrying games played before the 1863 code
a local habit that is not yet one printed world book

lessons.title: 26 October 1863 Again
lessons.mainIdea: The Football Association first met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London on 26 October 1863.
reading: Clubs met to agree on written rules for a kicking game. They formed the Football Association.
The meeting mattered because paper can travel. A club in a new town could copy the laws instead of guessing the local custom.
Rugby clubs that wanted carrying did not join that kicking code. Two sports kept two papers.

words.d: the group formed in London on 26 October 1863

lessons.title: IFAB Writes the Laws
lessons.mainIdea: The International Football Association Board writes the Laws of the Game.
reading: IFAB, not FIFA, is the keeper of the numbered Laws. Law 1 describes the field. Law 3 names eleven players. Law 5 names the referee.
FIFA organizes world competitions. The Laws are a different paper from a tournament poster.
A school pitch in Illinois can still be measured from Law 1 even when the match is only a gym-class rectangle.

words.d: the board that writes soccer's Laws of the Game
the numbered world rule book for soccer

lessons.title: FIFA in Paris, 1904
lessons.mainIdea: FIFA was founded in Paris on 21 May 1904 as a world association of national football bodies.
reading: Seven national associations met in Paris and formed FIFA. England's FA did not join that first day.
FIFA is an office of offices. It does not replace IFAB's Laws.
A world body made it easier to arrange matches across borders.

words.d: the world association for soccer, founded in Paris in 1904
a national or world body that joins clubs or countries

lessons.title: Uruguay, 1930
lessons.mainIdea: The first FIFA World Cup was played in Uruguay in 1930. Uruguay won.
reading: Thirteen teams entered. Games were played in Montevideo. Uruguay, the host, won the final against Argentina.
The trophy later took Jules Rimet's name. The tournament became soccer's largest national-team meet.
1930 is a world date. 1863 is the code date. 1904 is the office date.

words.d: FIFA's tournament among national teams, first held in 1930
the host and first champion in 1930

lessons.title: A Pitch Anyone Can Draw
lessons.mainIdea: Law 1 describes a rectangular field with goals. Two towns can mark that shape without sharing a language.
reading: The pitch has touchlines, goal lines, and a center mark. The goals face each other.
Paint does the introducing, the way a baseball diamond's bags do. The words in Law 1 tell a grounds crew what to paint.
A school field may be smaller than a World Cup pitch. The idea of a shared rectangle still holds.

words.d: the Law that describes the field of play

lessons.title: IHSA Boys Soccer, 1972
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA crowned its first boys soccer state champion in 1972.
reading: The IHSA began in 1900. Boys soccer as a state series crowned a first champion in 1972.
Schools and clubs played soccer in Illinois before that date. 1972 is statewide school paper.
The series uses school pitches the districts already mark.

lessons.title: IHSA Girls Soccer, 1988
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA crowned its first girls soccer state champion in 1988.
reading: Girls soccer in the IHSA crowned a first champion in 1988, sixteen years after the boys' first title.
The gap is about school series paper. Girls played soccer in clubs and schools before 1988.
1988 sits after Title IX in 1972, but the two papers are not the same document.

lessons.title: A School Pitch Is Still Law 1
lessons.mainIdea: An Illinois gym-class rectangle is a smaller cousin of the World Cup pitch.
reading: Teachers paint or cone a rectangle. Two goals or two cones stand at the ends.
The idea is Law 1 at school size: a shared shape, a ball, a referee or a teacher with a whistle.
The words still travel. The grass may be shorter. The code is the same family.

words.d: a smaller field that still follows the same idea
the sound tool that starts and stops play
